memories.content: Avoid em dashes in the proposal; split the sentence or use more ordinary punctuation instead.
The user tends to place several independently reviewable claims in one long sentence.
Use first-person active voice for choices and commitments owned by the proposal author so responsibility remains explicit throughout the work plan.
Describe prototype operations that have already been implemented and verified as observed states.
Describe prototype operations not yet implemented or evaluated as plans or expectations.
When a commitment is phrased passively, readers may interpret it as uncertainty, evasiveness, or reluctance to take responsibility.
Use “we” only for decisions and commitments the authors control, not for external facts or actions owned by another party.
The user should use one first-person pronoun consistently for the same authorial role and should not alternate between “I” and “we” unless the responsible party actually changes.
The user tends to hide unsettled commitments behind passive phrases such as “will be considered” or “is expected.”
Split proposal prose into short sentences when a sentence contains more than one independently reviewable claim.
Keep one main claim in each sentence so a reviewer can locate and assess it quickly.
The user tends to repeat em dashes when a sentence already contains several clauses.
Repeated em dashes can shift a reviewer’s attention from the proposal’s argument to suspicion that its prose was generated by AI.
Use an em dash only for a deliberate interruption or sharp contrast; otherwise split the sentence or choose ordinary punctuation.
In procedural passages, begin each sentence with the action, condition, or output instead of repeating “we” so the steps remain easy to follow and reuse.
Write system behaviors confirmed in the actual usage environment as observed states.
Write system behaviors not yet confirmed in the field as conditional plans.
Readers can reconstruct a sequence more accurately when each sentence begins with the action or condition rather than the author.
Do not mechanically split connected thoughts into separate short sentences when doing so destroys the intended reading rhythm.
Preserve a longer sentence when its clauses form one continuous movement that is easier to follow together than apart.
The user understands that short sentences are easier to scan but feels that uniformly segmented prose loses its reading rhythm.
Write procedural sentences so their opening phrase can be reused as a checklist item without changing the step's meaning.
The user should choose “I” as an individual author or “we” for a named team and should not mix them when describing the same responsible party.
Action-first procedural sentences can be reordered or copied into a checklist more easily because their subject is the step rather than the proposal author.
The user can explain whether an em dash marks an intentional interruption or contrast rather than using it decoratively.
An em dash creates a stronger interruption than a comma and can make a deliberate contrast easier to hear in the sentence.

options.label: Author first
options.text: Begin with “I” or “we” so responsibility for the commitment is explicit.

options.label: Action first
options.text: Begin with the action, condition, or output so the sentence functions directly as a procedural or checklist step.

options.label: Separate statements
options.text: State ownership in one sentence and express the reusable procedural step in another.

issues.question: When a procedural step is also an author-owned commitment, which element should its sentence foreground?
issues.title: Choose the opening for procedural commitments
issues.why_it_matters: The choice determines whether the prose prioritizes explicit accountability or reusable, sequence-oriented procedure structure.

analysis.overview: The frames largely align on disciplined proposal prose while preserving context-sensitive exceptions for punctuation, sentence rhythm, evidence maturity, and pronoun consistency. Their substantive unresolved difference concerns whether author-owned procedural commitments should foreground responsible authors or checklist-ready actions.

relations.reason: The deliberate-interruption or contrast condition explains and must preserve the compared frame’s narrower exception to the reference frame’s general avoidance policy.
relations.summary: The reference broadly avoids em dashes in proposals, while the compared frame permits them for intentional interruption or sharp contrast whose stronger effect the user can identify.

relations.reason: The policies govern different sentence structures: independent claims favor segmentation, whereas clauses forming one coherent movement may remain together.
relations.summary: The reference splits sentences containing independently reviewable claims, while the compared frame preserves connected clauses when separation would damage a continuous, readable rhythm.

relations.reason: A procedural sentence that is also an author-owned commitment falls under both rules, but cannot simultaneously begin with the responsible author and with the procedural step.
relations.summary: The reference requires author-owned choices and commitments to use explicit first-person active voice, while the compared frame requires procedural sentences to begin with reusable actions, conditions, or outputs rather than the author.

relations.reason: Prototype verification and field confirmation are explicit evidence scopes; a behavior may be reported as observed at the prototype level while remaining conditional as a field claim.
relations.summary: The reference classifies implemented and verified prototype operations as observed states and unevaluated ones as plans, while the compared frame reserves field-level observed-state claims for behavior confirmed in actual usage.

relations.reason: These memories form one one-sided observation linking a recurring passive-voice practice to its interpretive consequence; the compared frame provides no counterpart.
relations.summary: The reference identifies a tendency to conceal unsettled commitments in passive phrasing and warns that readers may perceive uncertainty, evasiveness, or reluctance to accept responsibility.

relations.reason: This ownership boundary is independently useful one-sided guidance not stated by the compared frame’s pronoun-consistency rule.
relations.summary: The reference restricts “we” to decisions and commitments controlled by the authors, excluding external facts and actions owned by others.

relations.reason: They express the same operational rule under the same scope: do not alternate first-person pronouns for one unchanged responsible party.
relations.summary: Both frames require choosing “I” or “we” according to the responsible authorial role and using that pronoun consistently unless the responsible party changes.

relations.reason: These memories state one one-sided pattern and its reviewer-facing consequence, neither of which is asserted by the compared frame.
relations.summary: The reference notes repeated em dashes in clause-heavy sentences and warns that they can distract reviewers from the argument by prompting suspicion of AI-generated prose.

reports.both: Both require a consistent first-person pronoun for the same responsible party.
reports.differences: They qualify em-dash use, sentence splitting, and observed-state language by different explicit contexts. They conflict on whether procedural commitments should open with the responsible author or the action.
reports.reference_only: The reference additionally warns about evasive passive commitments, limits “we” to author-controlled matters, and links repeated em dashes with reviewer distraction and AI suspicion.
